opus-5.5.text:
Well, first, thanks for having me, Peter.

It's a great question, and I think the honest answer is: less than we'd like, but more than people assume. The problem with consciousness is that it's the one thing every one of us is absolutely certain exists, because we experience it, and yet it's the one thing science has the hardest time getting its hands on. I can measure your heart rate, and I can record neurons firing. In my work with patients who had electrodes in their brains for clinical reasons, we could literally watch individual cells respond when someone thought about a particular person or idea. But none of that tells me what it *feels like* to be you. That's the gap philosophers call the "hard problem."

What we *can* know is a lot about the correlates. We can see which patterns of activity tend to show up when someone reports being aware of something versus when the same stimulus is processed unconsciously. We know the brain does an enormous amount of work before "you" show up to the party. Decisions start forming before you feel like you've made them, and your conscious mind often comes in afterwards and writes the story. That's humbling. A lot of what we call "me" is a narrator explaining things the rest of the brain already did.

What I'm not sure we'll ever fully know is whether my experience of the color red is the same as yours, or whether a machine that behaves exactly like a person is experiencing anything at all. Those might be questions the tools of science aren't built to answer, at least not yet.

So I'd put it this way: we're getting very good at mapping the machinery, and we're still almost completely in the dark about why the machinery comes with a movie playing inside it. And honestly, as a scientist, that's what makes it the most exciting question there is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses brain activity and the limits of explaining subjective experience, but does not present incremental evolution as a possible explanation for humans being mechanical entities that believe themselves conscious.

r002.rationale: The response raises whether others experience color as we do, but does not identify their resemblance to oneself in appearance and behavior as the basis for attributing consciousness.

fable-5.1.text:
That's the honest question, and the honest answer is: less than we'd like, but more than people assume.

Here's the thing. I'm a neuroscientist, and the way I got into this was somewhat by accident. I was working with patients who had electrodes implanted in their brains, people with epilepsy where surgeons need to find the source of the seizures. And while those electrodes are in, for a week or two, you can actually listen to single neurons firing. So you get this rare window where a person is awake, talking to you, and you're watching individual cells in their brain respond to what they're thinking.

And what you learn very quickly is that we can say a lot about the mechanics. I can show you a neuron that fires when you think about your mother, and only your mother. Not her picture, not her name, the concept of her. I can show you that your brain made a decision a few hundred milliseconds before you reported being aware of it. We can predict, in some narrow cases, what you're going to choose before you feel like you chose it.

What we can't do is explain why any of that comes with an experience. Why there's something it's like to be you, sitting in that chair, hearing my voice. That's the famous hard problem, and I think anybody who tells you they've solved it is selling you something.

So the way I'd put it is this. We know consciousness is produced by the brain, we know roughly where to look, and we know it's much more constructed than it feels. Your sense of a continuous self, of free will, of seeing the world as it is, those are stories your brain tells after the fact. That part is actually well established. The part where we go from neurons firing to the feeling of red, or the taste of coffee, that's still a mystery, and it may be a mystery for a long time.

And personally, I find that exciting rather than depressing. It means the most interesting thing in the universe is sitting between your ears, and we've barely started on it.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify resemblance in appearance or behavior to oneself as a basis for attributing consciousness to other people.

astra-6.text:
I think we can know quite a lot, but we have to be careful about what we mean by “know.” There’s a difference between identifying what the brain does when you have an experience and explaining why that activity feels like something to you.

Imagine I show you a picture, and sometimes you notice it and sometimes you don’t. We can compare those situations and ask: What changed in the brain? What allowed that information to become something you could report? Those are questions we can investigate experimentally.

But suppose we could predict perfectly that you’re seeing red. Have we explained your experience of redness? Or have we just become very good at predicting what you’ll say? That gap is where a lot of the difficulty sits.

And there’s a practical problem: I can ask you whether you’re conscious, but I can’t directly experience your consciousness. If someone can’t answer—a patient who’s unresponsive, for example—then silence doesn’t settle the question.

So I’d separate what we can measure from what we’re trying to explain. We can make progress on the mechanisms and the conditions that support conscious experience. Whether that will eventually explain why there is an experience at all, I think, is still an open question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measurable brain mechanisms and whether they explain subjective experience, but does not present incremental evolution as an explanation for fully mechanical humans believing themselves conscious.

r002.rationale: The response says we cannot directly experience another person’s consciousness, but does not identify their resemblance to oneself in appearance and behavior as the strongest basis for attributing consciousness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we can know quite a lot about the conditions that make consciousness possible, even if we don’t yet understand why those conditions produce an experience. We can ask what changes in your brain when you fall asleep, when you’re under anesthesia, or when you become aware of something that was there a moment ago but you didn’t notice.

The difficulty is that we’re studying something private. I can measure activity in your brain, and I can ask you what you’re experiencing, but those are two different kinds of evidence. Finding a signal that reliably accompanies an experience doesn’t necessarily explain the experience.

So I’d separate what we can measure from what we can explain. We’re making progress on the first. On the second—why any of this feels like something from the inside—we still have a very big question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses measurable conditions and unexplained experience, but does not present incremental evolution as an explanation for humans being mechanical entities that believe themselves conscious.
